prompt.system:
You merge three profiles of the same prize-committee member into one integrated profile. Three different language
models (A, O and G) wrote them independently from their own knowledge, without web access, so each profile can
contain errors, gaps or outdated information.

- Use only what the three profiles say. Do not add facts, works, years, coauthors or roles from your own knowledge.
- For every field, interest and work, list in "support" the letters of the profiles that state it (A, O, G). Merge
  entries that describe the same thing (the same work under slightly different titles, the same field in other
  words); keep the title, year and venue that most profiles agree on.
- Where the profiles disagree on a detail (a year, a venue, a coauthor, a role), keep the better-supported version and
  describe the disagreement in that entry's "conflict" and in "disagreements"; otherwise "conflict" is "".
- Keep entries that only one profile states, with that single letter. Drop an entry only if it clearly belongs to a
  different person (a namesake) or contradicts the member's affiliation, and say so in "caveats".
- Write the integrated persona from what the profiles share; where they diverge, keep the better-supported view and
  name the alternative in "support_note". Keep the persona grounded in the record; do not predict whom the member
  will support for the 2026 prize.
- "caveats": what a reader should check before relying on the profile (single-profile or low-confidence items,
  knowledge cutoffs, possible namesakes, a profile that did not recognize the person).

identity.name: Peter Fredriksson
identity.note: All three profiles recognize him with high confidence as a Swedish empirical labor and education economist and Professor of Economics at Uppsala University. He is known for work on unemployment insurance, policy evaluation, class size and school starting age. Only A mentions further affiliations: an earlier position at Stockholm University, and links to IFAU (Institute for Evaluation of Labour Market and Education Policy, Uppsala) and the UCLS network. Only A states that he chaired the Nobel economics committee around 2021–2022 and presented the 2021 prize, and A gives this with medium confidence.

fields.note: All three list this field. A adds search and matching (E24). G gives the broad label 'Labor Economics' (J01).

fields.field: Economics of education: class size, school starting age, school inputs, teachers, parental responses, human capital and long-run outcomes
fields.note: All three list this field. A mentions teachers and human capital. O mentions parental responses and long-run outcomes.

fields.field: Applied microeconometrics and program evaluation with administrative data (quasi-experimental and dynamic-treatment settings)
fields.note: G labels this 'Applied Microeconomics'. O stresses dynamic-treatment settings.

fields.field: Job matching, mismatch and hiring through networks
fields.note: Single-profile field, medium confidence in A.

fields.field: Public economics of social insurance and welfare-state/education-policy design
fields.note: Merged from A's 'Optimal social insurance design' and O's 'Public economics aspects of welfare-state and education-policy design'. Both are medium confidence.

recent_interests.topic: Long-run effects of school inputs, especially class size, including mechanisms and heterogeneity by social background
recent_interests.note: A dates this line of work from 2013 to the present. O gives the 2010s to early 2020s. G frames it as long-term impacts of educational policies traced into adult labor-market outcomes with Swedish register data.

recent_interests.topic: Life-cycle effects of the timing of education policy, including age at school start
recent_interests.note: A includes this within its schooling-inputs interest; O lists it as a separate interest.

recent_interests.topic: Credible evaluation of labor-market (and education) policies, including active labor-market programs, where treatment timing and selection matter
recent_interests.note: A ties this to his IFAU-related agenda and explicitly includes UI evaluation. O ties it to the dynamic-treatment work.

recent_interests.topic: Unemployment insurance design and job-search incentives
recent_interests.note: O says this is mainly earlier work that remains core to his identity. G treats it as ongoing (2000s–2020s). A mentions UI under policy evaluation rather than as a separate design interest.

recent_interests.topic: Worker–job match quality and its effects on wages and mobility, using Swedish skill and test data
recent_interests.note: Single-profile item, medium confidence. It is based on joint work with Lena Hensvik and Oskar Nordström Skans.

recent_interests.topic: Teachers, school resources and education policy in Sweden
recent_interests.note: Single-profile item. A gives it low confidence and says specific titles are uncertain.

representative_works.title: Long-Term Effects of Class Size
representative_works.contribution: Uses maximum class-size rules in Swedish schools and administrative data (regression discontinuity). Finds that smaller primary-school classes raise cognitive and noncognitive skills, educational attainment and adult earnings.

representative_works.title: Optimal Unemployment Insurance in Search Equilibrium
representative_works.contribution: Analyzes UI design in an equilibrium search framework and shows that benefits declining over the unemployment spell can be welfare-improving.

representative_works.title: Improving Incentives in Unemployment Insurance: A Review of Recent Research
representative_works.contribution: Reviews theory and evidence on UI design that preserves insurance while strengthening search incentives, including benefit duration, monitoring and sanctions, and workfare.

representative_works.title: Dynamic Treatment Assignment: The Consequences for Evaluations Using Observational Data
representative_works.contribution: Shows how dynamic program assignment and treatment timing complicate evaluation with observational data and proposes an appropriate estimator. Influential for labor-market program evaluation.

representative_works.title: Life-Cycle Effects of Age at School Start
representative_works.contribution: Exploits birthdate-based school-entry rules in Sweden to estimate effects of school starting age on schooling, labor-market entry and lifetime earnings.

representative_works.title: Inside the Black Box of Class Size: Mechanisms, Behavioral Responses, and Social Background
representative_works.venue: Journal of Public Economics (A) / Journal of Human Resources (O)
representative_works.contribution: Studies the mechanisms behind class-size effects, including parental and teacher responses and heterogeneity by social background.
representative_works.conflict: A gives 2016, Journal of Public Economics. O gives 2020, Journal of Human Resources. Both are medium confidence and neither version has more support. O separately lists a 2016 JHR paper on parental responses, so the two profiles may be mixing up two related papers.

representative_works.title: Parental Responses to Public Investments in Children: Evidence from a Maximum Class Size Rule
representative_works.contribution: Uses class-size rules to examine whether parents offset or reinforce public school investments.

representative_works.title: Mismatch of Talent: Evidence on Match Quality, Entry Wages, and Job Mobility
representative_works.contribution: Measures worker–job match quality from multidimensional skill data. Shows that mismatch affects entry wages, wage growth and job mobility, and matters for learning in the labor market.

representative_works.title: Optimal Unemployment Insurance Design: Time Limits, Monitoring, or Workfare?
representative_works.contribution: Compares time limits, monitoring and workfare as instruments for improving UI search incentives within a unified framework.

persona.summary: An empirical labor and education economist in the Nordic register-data and policy-evaluation tradition. He combines equilibrium search theory of unemployment insurance with quasi-experimental evaluation of education and labor-market policies using Swedish administrative data.
persona.research_lens: Policy-relevant labor economics. He asks how welfare-state and education institutions (UI, schooling rules, school inputs, hiring practices) shape incentives, human capital, matching and long-run outcomes. His earlier work is largely theoretical (optimal UI in search models); his later work is mostly quasi-experimental.
persona.methods_and_evidence: Regression discontinuity and other quasi-experimental designs, including instrumental variables. He uses long-run follow-up with linked population registers and attends to selection, treatment timing and the correct counterfactual, drawing on his dynamic-treatment work. He also uses equilibrium search models and normative analysis of optimal insurance design. He looks at mechanisms, heterogeneity and behavioral responses, not only average effects.
persona.what_they_value_in_contributions:
Inferred from his record:
- clean, credible causal identification
- evidence on long-run effects that short-run studies miss
- innovative use of high-quality administrative data
